title: Interleaved Tensor+Pipeline Sharding — proposal and ops notes
body:
Purpose
-------
This working doc proposes an interleaved tensor/pipeline sharding strategy for the serving runtime that optimizes for low p99 latency on short-context interactive workloads while retaining high tokens/sec for long-streaming workloads. It combines: (1) fine-grained tensor-parallel sharding for large linear weights, (2) pipeline parallelism for attention + MLP stage separation on very large models, and (3) KV-cache sharding keyed to the execution pattern to reduce cross-GPU collectives.

Scope and goals
---------------
- Target hardware: 4–16 GPUs per model instance (mix of A100/H100 with NVLink where available).
- Workloads: chat/assistant interactive (short sequences, many concurrent sessions), embeddings/streaming (longer sequences but tolerant to higher throughput).
- SLOs: p50 <= 50ms for single-turn short context (<= 128 tokens) on 4-GPU configs; p99 degradation acceptable up to 2x for very large models but must not exceed 1s for interactive flows.
- Constraints: limited cross-host RDMA for some Dedicated customers; transparent fallback to hosted variants; zero-downtime model rollouts.

Design summary (short)
---------------------
1) Partition weights by tensor parallel groups (TP) using chunked linear slices aligned to CUDA/HBM boundaries.
2) When model size exceeds per-GPU memory, create 2–stage pipeline segments (P) where attention layers are grouped to stage A and MLP layers to stage B; use micro-batching to keep pipeline bubbles small.
3) KV cache is sharded by layer and head-range (kv-shard per (layer, head-span)) to localize reads during autoregressive decoding; global synchronizations only when needed for cross-layer reduction (rare).
4) Use reduce-scatter + allgather patterns rather than naive all-reduce for activation exchanges in TP to reduce memory amplification.
5) Carefully tune NCCL: chunk sizes, CUDA stream concurrency, and use of NCCL graphs to reduce launch overheads.

Why interleaved?
----------------
- Pure tensor-parallel approaches hurt memory-bound KV caches (large past-length -> KV blowup).
- Pure pipeline-only causes long tail latency when micro-batches are small.
- Interleaving gives us the ability to localize most KV accesses (reducing cross-GPU reads) while letting weights be split across GPUs to fit large models.

Detailed components
-------------------
A) Weight placement and kernel mapping
- Linear weights: shard across TP group with contiguous column-major slices sized to maintain coalesced loads (prefer 256KB+ chunks).
- Attention q/k/v projections: colocate q and k local halves so that KV cache writes are local; v can be colocated with downstream MLP if pipeline split favors that.
- Fused kernels: use fused qkv kernel when layers are fully local; fall back to separate kernels when TP splits cross the qkv boundary.
- Custom CUDA kernels should expose an "async-comm" boundary where data for reduce-scatter is emitted into pinned staging buffers to overlap with compute.

B) KV-cache sharding strategy
- Primary key: (layer_id, head_block_id). Choose head_block size to be a tunable knob (defaults: 4 heads per shard).
- Each shard stores K/V tensors for only its heads. During decode, each token step reads only the head-local KV slices and performs local matmuls.
- For attention patterns that require cross-head interaction (rare for standard transformer), we fall back to an allgather of small per-token context vectors.
- Eviction: LRU based per-shard with async flush-to-SSD option for very long contexts on Dedicated/private.
- Checkpointing: periodic async checkpoint of KV-shards to local SSD every N steps (configurable). This allows quick reload on preempt/restart within a single host.

C) Communication patterns and NCCL tuning
- Use reduce-scatter + local compute + allgather for TP weight-exchange pattern. This reduces peak memory compared to all-reduce.
- Chunking: tune chunk size to balance latency vs bw utilization. Empirically we see good throughput with 512KB–4MB chunks for H100 NVLink rings; for inter-host RDMA rings prefer 1MB–8MB.
- Stream concurrency: dedicate one high-priority CUDA stream for NCCL launches; use additional worker streams for kernel compute and pre/post processing. Avoid launching small NCCL ops on the default stream.
- NCCL graphs: for steady-state streaming workloads, capture NCCL graph per model topology and reuse to reduce launch overheads. This is especially helpful when micro-batches are 1 or 2.
- P2P vs Ring: prefer NVLink P2P when on single host; on multi-host clusters prefer ring with reduce-scatter since RDMA rings achieve better cross-host stability.
- Async progress: enable CUDA Cooperative Threads / background progress where supported to reduce stalls on small messages.

D) Scheduler and runtime choices
- Work unit: request -> micro-batches -> token steps. Scheduler decides mapping of micro-batches to pipeline stages and TP groups.
- Dynamic packing: pack multiple short sessions into a single micro-batch to amortize kernel overhead. Keep an LRU packer tuned per model and per workload class.
- Affinity: prefer keeping an interactive session pinned to the same TP group and pipeline slot to maximize KV locality. Migration must transfer KV shards (prefer async copy) and be rate limited.
- Preemption: on heavy contention, evict least-recently-used sessions by checkpointing KV and responding with fallback model variant (smaller model/less parallel).

E) Failure and degradation modes
- GPU loss (single-GPU failure in multi-GPU group): try fast-rebuild by pulling model shards from peer replicas; if unavailable, failover to hosted model with token-level span mapping (best-effort) and resume session.
- NCCL call failure: instrument and fast-fail to retry with doubled chunk sizes or slower ring. Escalate to fallback if repeated.
- KV corruption: use versioned KV shards with short-lived checksums; repair by replaying tokens from client if necessary (requires client support).

Experiment plan (what to measure)
---------------------------------
- Microbench 1: 4-GPU, 8-head-blocks KV-shard config. Measure p50/p95/p99 latency for 1, 4, 16 concurrent sessions at seq length 32 and 128.
- Microbench 2: 8-GPU pipeline split (A: 12 layers, B: 12 layers) with varying micro-batch sizes (1–8). Capture pipeline bubble % and effective tokens/sec.
- Comm bench: measure NCCL bandwidth and latency vs chunk size on representative topology (NVLink vs RDMA). Record GPU utilization and stall time.
- Failure bench: kill GPU 1 in a 4-GPU set mid-session, measure time-to-recover and token loss.

Rollout / staged validation
---------------------------
1) Dev: run model smoke on dev infra with synthetic traffic. Validate correctness of shard assembly and KV reads.
2) Canary: small traffic slice on Dedicated cluster with same CPU/GPU SKU. Monitor p99, KV hit rate, NCCL errors.
3) Beta customers: invite 2–3 customers running interactive chat (low-sensitivity data) to run under opt-in.
4) GA: global rollout with automatic telemetry gating.

Open questions / TODOs
---------------------
- Should we implement head-block size as static per-model or adaptive at runtime based on observed per-head sparsity? (Priya to prototype adaptive head grouping — INF-1376).
- Cost accounting: how to meter tokens when sessions migrate across instances? Need billing hooks for partial-serving.
- Inter-host bandwidth variability: add jitter-aware chunking to cope with noisy neighbors on shared clouds.
- Investigate CUDA IPC for within-host cross-process KV transfers to speed up session migrations.

Notes to reviewers
------------------
- This is intentionally pragmatic: we prefer complexity in the runtime (scheduling + KV placement) over model surgery. That keeps developer interface stable.
- Look for areas where we can re-use existing code paths (batching/packer, KV store) and where we must introduce new APIs (kv-shard map, migration primitives).

Appendix: quick config knobs (defaults)
--------------------------------------
- head_block_size: "4"
- kv_checkpoint_steps: "2000"
- kv_eviction_policy: "async_lru"
- nccL_chunk_target_bytes: "1048576"
- pipeline_microbatch_max: "8"

References and links
--------------------
- Related RFCs: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/1482
- Prior notes: internal doc hybrid-sharding-kv-scheduler-notes.json (see Drive)
- Slack threads: #serving-runtime: "kv-shard mapping" (Dec 2025)

End of doc.

Unresolved: lots of small optimizations (kernel fusion heuristics, chunk-size autotuner) but the high-level shape is stable.
